title: eRevise: Using Natural Language Processing to Provide Formative Feedback on Text Evidence Usage in Student Writing
extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether an automated writing evaluation system can provide useful formative feedback to help students revise essays, specifically improving their use of textual evidence in response-to-text writing. The broader motivation is that automated essay scoring often produces scores without actionable guidance, whereas revision quality may improve if students receive feedback aligned to a writing rubric. The study does not concern ChatGPT or large language models, and it is not a high-school comparative trial; instead, it evaluates an NLP-based feedback system for upper-elementary and early middle-school writing.

The intervention is eRevise, a web-based system that collects a first draft, analyzes it using rubric-aligned natural language processing features, and then displays two prewritten feedback messages tailored to the student's detected needs. The feedback focuses on evidence use, such as adding more evidence, making evidence more specific, explaining evidence, and connecting evidence to the main idea. Students then revise their essays in a second class period. The automated feedback is based on features such as number of evidence topics and specificity of examples drawn from the source text.

The pilot deployment involved 143 students in seven grade 5 and 6 English Language Arts classrooms in two rural parishes in Louisiana, United States. The writing task asked students to respond to an article about the Millennium Villages Project in Kenya by arguing whether fighting poverty is achievable in our lifetime, supported with 3-4 examples from the text. Outcomes included human-scored Evidence rubric scores and NLP-derived indicators of evidence quantity and specificity before and after revision.

The authors conclude that students showed modest improvement after receiving automated formative feedback and revising. Human-scored Evidence rubric scores increased slightly with trending significance, and automated indicators of number of evidence pieces and specificity improved significantly. Improvements were strongest for students whose initial drafts had less sophisticated evidence use. However, this was a single-group pre/post pilot without a control condition, over only two class periods, so causal claims are limited. For the user's target review question, this is a near-miss exclusion: it is not grades 9-12, not an LLM/ChatGPT system, and not a comparative study against teacher, peer, or no-feedback control.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a pilot single-group pre/post classroom deployment without a control group, randomization, or quasi-experimental comparison. It provides suggestive empirical evidence but does not meet stronger causal credibility standards.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings are directionally positive but small and incompletely reported, with no standardized effect sizes and only trend-level improvement on the primary human-scored writing outcome. Impact is therefore modest or unclear.

interventions.use_case: NLP-based automated formative feedback on elementary students’ response-to-text essay drafts, specifically targeting quantity, relevance, specificity, and explanation of textual evidence during revision.

finding.finding_summary: This paper reports a single-group pre/post pilot deployment of eRevise in 7 classrooms with grades 5-6 students (n=143), not a comparative study and not grades 9-12. Human-scored Evidence rubric scores improved from M=2.62 (SD=0.95) on first drafts to M=2.72 (SD=0.92) on revised drafts with trend-level significance (paired t-test, p<=0.08); NLP-derived evidence-use indicators also improved, with NPE increasing from M=2.61 (SD=1.27) to M=2.81 (SD=1.08), p<=0.003, and SPC Total Merged from M=9.65 (SD=4.94) to M=11.15 (SD=5.39), p<=0.001. No standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Human-scored RTA Evidence rubric scores on response-to-text essays; NLP features approximating evidence quantity (NPE) and specificity/relevance (SPC Total Merged) before vs after revision
finding.std_deviation: First-draft Evidence SD=0.95; second-draft Evidence SD=0.92; first-draft NPE SD=1.27; second-draft NPE SD=1.08; first-draft SPC Total Merged SD=4.94; second-draft SPC Total Merged SD=5.39
